newsitem.title: GERMANY: German markets unsettled by debt forecasts, U.S.
newsitem.headline: German markets unsettled by debt forecasts, U.S.

text.p: A warning that Germany would fail to meet debt and deficit criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) helped unsettle domestic financial markets on Tuesday, analysts said.

Forecasts from the country's six leading economic research institutes predicted the German public sector deficit would amount to 3.5 percent of economic output in 1997, well above the Maastricht Treaty's three percent goal.

The bi-annual forecast also said German interest rates may need to rise if money supply growth remained above target levels, a conclusion that immediately sent the German mark rising against the dollar.
But the comments undermined German bonds and shares, which have been buoyed by strong gains in U.S. markets and hopes that German interest rates would continue to fall.
"The institute's forecast is an unsettling factor for the markets," Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at German investment house Trinkaus & Burkhardt said.

Attempts by German finance minister Theo Waigel to offer reassurance that Germany's 1997 budget deficit would be within Maastricht goals fell on deaf ears after a Bundesbank council member appeared to support the institutes' forecasts.
Speaking in London, Hans-Juergen Koebnick said that he feared the forecast that Germany would miss the EMU criteria was realistic.

The DTB Bund future slipped 25 basis points lower to 99.10 in early trade before recovering slightly to 99.21. The benchmark 6.25 percent 2006 Bund meanwhile slipped to 101.29, yielding 6.05 percent, against Monday's close of 101.47.
Trinkaus' Kricks-Brunnlieb noted that European bond markets had been supported in recent months by optimism that the single European currency would be launched on time in 1999.
But some analysts pointed out that the forecast on deficit levels was not in itself a shock.
"The forecast is broadly in line with expectations, so the bond market impact should not be too great," said Brian Clapp, an analyst at London-based Stone & McCarthy.
Tuesday's Bund weakness was also seen as being based on uncertainty ahead key U.S. jobs data due on Friday.

The prospect of even a long-term tightening in German interest rates sent the mark higher against the dollar, with the U.S. currency at one point falling to 1.5080 to the mark against Monday's European closing level of just under 1.5180.
"The market is very much coming to the feeling that maybe we're not going to get any more cuts in interest rates," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at London-based Bank of Boston.
The U.S. currency later gained slightly to trade at around 1.5100 against the mark in early afternoon.
German shares, already lower in line with Wall Street's overnight weakness, also took an indirect hit from the lower bond market and the easier dollar.

The German DAX index of top 30 shares traded 30.46 points or 1.13 percent lower at 2,683.52 just before bourse close as dealers said the institutes' forecast had put further pressure on a market that was already in a phase of consolidation.
But they added that unless the dollar fell further -- a drag on Germany's many export-driven stocks -- any further decline in the equity market was not expected to be great.
"The DAX is supported around 2,670-80, so we should be able to bounce off," said one German share dealer.
